newsitem.title: UK: N Ireland unionists may agree to new peace plan.
newsitem.headline: N Ireland unionists may agree to new peace plan.

text.p: Leaders of the main pro-British unionist party in Northern Ireland indicated on Tuesday that they might be able to accept new Anglo-Irish proposals to achieve progress in deadlocked peace talks.

The proposals, designed to enable the IRA to call a ceasefire and its political wing, Sinn Fein, to join all-party talks on the province's future, are to be announced by British Prime Minister Tony Blair to parliament on Wednesday.
David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionists, the main Protestant party in the province, his deputy John Taylor and senior MP Ken Maginnis met Blair for 1-1/4 hours on Tuesday to discuss the plan.

When he emerged from Blair's Downing Street office, Trimble told reporters the plan involved the concept of "parallel decommissioning" by which the IRA would start to give up its huge cache of arms as the talks proceeded.
Under the previous Conservative government, Britain insisted on a renewed Irish Republican Army ceasefire and at least a start on the handover of weapons before Sinn Fein could join in talks.

But Blair is hoping that by making lighter demands he can persuade the IRA to resume the ceasefire they abandoned in February 1996, committing themselves to political methods to work towards their goal of a united Ireland.

The Roman Catholic IRA has been waging a guerrilla campaign since 1969 to end British rule in Northern Ireland and merge it with the Irish Republic. Northern Ireland's Protestant majority favours continued union with Britain.
Trimble said parallel decommissioning was not his party's "first preference". But he added: "We indicated that we could go along...provided of course that that is what actually happened."
He said there could be no question of Sinn Fein making vague promises in order to get into the talks, and mechanisms which ensured that arms were handed over would have to be in place.
Trimble said Blair had not actually shown him the 12-page document which he has agreed with Irish Prime Minister John Bruton as the basis for a drive to get talks moving.

However, Ian Paisley, leader of the smaller and more hardline Democratic Unionist Party, accused the British and Irish governments of having "given in to the IRA", and said his party might quit the all party talks.

Speaking on Irish radio, Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams said he had also not yet seen the proposals. "When we do see them, Sinn Fein will study very carefully the proposals that they are putting forward," he said.

Bruton, in New York with Blair on Monday for a United Nations environment summit, told Irish broadcasting network RTE that the agreement would create conditions for rapid movement in multi-party talks taking place in Belfast.
Blair said in New York that a possible way out of the impasse had been agreed.
"I think it's possible that we have the basis of a way forward. But of course this has got to be agreed with all the other parties," he told reporters.

Blair said all possible clarification had now been provided to Sinn Fein, which now had to choose between the political path and the dual approach of political action and violence that it had been pursuing.
Northern Ireland's "Troubles" represent one of the world's longest-running guerrilla conflicts, killing more than 3,200 people over the past 28 years.
